chapter_title: The Sermon at Benares & For Anne Gregory

mind_map.root_topic: Chapter 8: Enlightenment, Universal Mortality & Pure Love

branches.theme: Prose Narrative: The Sermon at Benares

details: Prince Siddhartha is shielded from life's miseries until age 25, when he sees four sights: a sick man, an aged man, a funeral procession, and a begging monk.
Renounces royalty, wanders for 7 years, meditates under a peepal tree (Bodhi Tree) for 7 days at Bodh Gaya, and becomes the Buddha.
Preaches his first sermon at the sacred city of Benares on the Ganges.
evidence_or_examples: The Four Sights triggering renunciation of princehood.

sub_branches.concept: Kisa Gotami and the Parable of Mustard Seeds
details: Kisa Gotami's only son dies; grief-stricken, she seeks medicine to revive him.
Buddha instructs her to fetch mustard seeds from a home where no parent, child, husband, or friend has ever died.
Her search across the city yields no such home, as every family has lost loved ones.
evidence_or_examples: People telling Gotami: 'The living are few, but the dead are many.'

details: Sitting by the road watching city lights flicker out, Gotami realizes human lives flicker and extinguish similarly.
Buddha teaches that life of mortals is brief and combined with pain.
Uses analogies: ripe fruits in constant danger of falling; earthen vessels made by potters bound to break.
Surrendering selfish grief and accepting impermanence brings peace of mind.
evidence_or_examples: Quote: 'He who has drawn out the arrow of lamentation... will obtain peace of mind.'

branches.theme: Poetic Study: For Anne Gregory by W.B. Yeats

details: A young man tells Anne Gregory that suitors love her for her striking golden hair ('honey-coloured ramparts') rather than her inner self.
Anne suggests she can dye her hair brown, black, or carrot so men love her character alone.
The speaker cites an old religious text stating that only God can love a person purely for themselves regardless of physical appearance.
evidence_or_examples: Lines: 'Only God, my dear, / Could love you for yourself alone / And not your yellow hair.'
